newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurobourses tumble - eye Sunday's French vote.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurobourses tumble - eye Sunday's French vote.

text.p: Major European bourses tumbled on Friday but the dollar benefited as investors, nervous about the future of European Monetary Union, anxously awaited the outcome of Sunday's French elections.

The dollar remained in favour as plans for a 1999 launch of the euro -- and the strength of the currency if it is launched -- were thrown further into doubt by the clash between Bonn and the Bundesbank this week and what is perceived as an increase in the the possibility that the opposition socialists will win power in France.
Frankfurt shares had tumbled around 2.3 percent by late-morning as German markets reacted sharply after their holiday on Thursday to the row over revaluing German gold assets

On the Paris bourse, leading stocks, which have suffered badly from election jitters over the past few days, shed more than 1.5 percent within the first 10 minutes of trading, though they clawed back some of their losses by late morning.
"Once again, a number of people are coming round to a probable Socialist victory," said a broker.
One victim, defence and electronics giant Thomson-CSF, was hit by prospects that the left, if it wins the election, may scrap the sale of the state's 58 percent stake.

In London blue chips managed to open moderately higher but profit-taking soon pushed them down into negative territory ahead of a weekend which, analysts said, may decide the fate of the single currency. The FTSE 100 index was at session lows by late morning, about 40 points down.
There was a view in London that a French leftwing victory at the weekend could spook bond and share markets throughout Europe on Monday.

"If the Socialists win (in France) there is bound to be a knee-jerk reaction in French and German bond and share markets on Monday which will spill over into our market," the head of trading at a major London brokerage said.
The listing on Monday of the Halifax building society, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, should prop up the financial sector helping to limit the downside, he said.
"The institutions have to have Halifax in their portfolios and the market knows it...But even that won't be enough to keep the FTSE afloat if the EMU turmoil continues."

On the foreign exchange front the dollar (along with sterling) continued to be supported by its role as a safe-haven currency. By 1100 GMT it was trading at 1.7 marks, up from 1.6990 in late Europe on Thursday. Against the yen, the dollar was trading at 116.30 yen against 116.12 late Thursday.

"The problems between the Bundesbank and the German government continue," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston, adding that he expected pressure for German Finance Minister Theo Waigle's resignation to mount.
The dollar is set to benefit as as long as the German gold revaluation plan, which would help Germany cut back its deficits to make the grade for EMU, remains an issue, said analysts.

"There's a lot of uncertainties concerning the gold and currency valuation plan of the Bundesbank...But we still have to wait for a vote in the lower house in Germany which intends to change the Bundesbank law," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7 marks and 116.30 yen compared with 1.6990 marks and 116.12 yen in late European trading on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 35 points at 4,636.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 20.5 points at 2,558.7.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 81 points at 3555.
PRECIOUS METALS Gold fixed firmer at $345.75 versus a London close on Thursday of $344.05. Silver was also firmer at $4.86.
